newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia faces crucial week for space programme.
newsitem.headline: Russia faces crucial week for space programme.

text.p: Russian experts, facing one of the toughest weeks in the long history of Moscow's space programme, will meet on Monday to decide when cosmonauts will fix the damaged Mir space station.

Mir has been limping around the Earth with reduced power since a cargo tug collided with the sprawling station on June 25, puncturing its Spektr science module and damaging energy-giving solar panels.

It was the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history and another blow to the prestige of the Russian Space Agency, which took responsibility for the programme after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and has since come under severe financial pressure.
"Tomorrow a state commission (tackling the crisis) will decide the final date for going into the Spektr module," the duty officer at Mission Control outside Moscow told Reuters on Sunday.
"At the moment we think it will take place in the night from July 17 to 18," said the officer, who declined to be named.
Russian space officials have already given this date as the preferred timing for delicate repair work on the station but have hitherto said the date could be shifted.
The future of Mir depends on the cosmonauts' repairs.

The officer said the two Russian cosmonauts, Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, and British-born NASA astronaut Michael Foale would spend part of Sunday preparing for the repairs, then speak to their families.
"The cosmonauts will clear equipment to make room for the work," he said.
Mir lost about half its power in the collision. The aim is for a cosmonaut to reattach 17 internal cables during the repairs and so restore power from some of Spektr's solar panels.
On Tuesday, the crew plans a dress rehearsal of their difficult repair job, which involves donning space suits inside the Mir and practising linking the cables.
The officer said the Russians would talk to their families by a video link and Foale to his family in the United States by telephone. The calls are private and Mission Control does not listen in.
New transmitters sent up as part of a cargo shipment last week will not only help the crew speak to their families but also to ground control during the repair work.

During the repairs a cosmonaut will install a new hatch separating the Spektr from Mir's other cluttered array of modules. Unlike the old hatch, the new one can be closed without requiring the cables to the solar panels to be unplugged.

But the repair is expected to be difficult as the Russian cosmonaut doing the work, with a second in reserve nearby, will be dressed in a bulky spacesuit and be operating in a cramped interior area of the station.
Foale will sit in the Soyuz escape module during the work.
